definition: Customer lifetime value (CLV or LTV) estimates the value a customer contributes over the full relationship with a business.
extendedDefinition: CLV estimates the economic value of a customer relationship, but the calculation depends on the business model and the inputs available. A simple revenue-based estimate multiplies average revenue per customer by the expected relationship length; a margin-based model also accounts for the cost of serving that customer. Teams should state whether the estimate uses revenue or gross profit, which cohort it covers, and how refunds, discounts, expansion, and churn are treated. Comparing CLV with customer acquisition cost can help evaluate acquisition efficiency, but the time horizon and assumptions must match. For software selection, verify that analytics tools expose cohort retention and revenue data needed to update the estimate rather than relying on a static lifetime assumption.
examples: A subscription business with $50 average monthly revenue per account and an estimated 18-month relationship calculates a simple revenue-based CLV of $900 before costs.
A finance team calculates margin-based CLV separately for small-business and enterprise customers because support and implementation costs differ.
A growth team compares acquisition cost and cohort-based CLV over the same 12-month window before increasing paid acquisition spend.
description: Customer lifetime value estimates the revenue or profit a customer contributes over time. Learn common calculation methods, assumptions, and how CLV relates to acquisition cost and retention.
